title: Dying Stars Can Kick Themselves Across Space
hook: A dying star flinging off lopsided blobs of gas nudges itself with each one — thousands of tiny kicks that add up to a getaway of about a kilometer per second.
key_points: As Sun-like stars swell into red giants, they shed gas in uneven, chaotic blobs rather than smooth shells.
Each lopsided ejection recoils the star the opposite way — Newton's third law, like a slow-motion rocket.
A single kick is only a few meters per second, but ~10,000 of them over hundreds of thousands of years can build to about 1 km/s.
These accumulated kicks can unbind wide binary star pairs, flinging companions apart.
In rare cases the nudges could steer two stars into a collision, triggering an explosion.
content_html: We tend to picture a Sun-like star ending its life quietly — puffing off its outer layers into a pretty planetary nebula before settling down as a white dwarf. But that shedding may not be nearly as gentle, or as symmetric, as the tidy images suggest.
extra_html: Caltech theoretical astrophysicist Jim Fuller, with input from Kareem El-Badry, argues that as these stars balloon into red giants, they eject gas in chaotic, lopsided blobs rather than smooth shells. Every uneven burst recoils the star in the opposite direction — Newton's third law, playing out like a very slow rocket. Any single kick is tiny, just a few meters per second (Fuller likens it to a human jogging pace), but a dying star may deliver something like 10,000 of them over several hundred thousand years. Summed up, they can push the star to roughly a kilometer per second. That's enough to matter: the accumulated shove can unbind wide binary systems, separating stars that had orbited each other for eons, and in rare cases could nudge two stars onto a collision course, ending in an explosion. The work was presented at the 248th meeting of the American Astronomical Society and submitted to Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific.

related.hook: Stars are born in collapsing gas clouds, spend their lives fusing hydrogen into helium, then die in ways that depend entirely on how heavy they are.

flashcards.prompt: What gives a dying Sun-like star a push through space?

choices.text: Uneven, asymmetric ejections of gas that recoil the star the opposite way, like a slow rocket
The gravitational pull of a passing planet
Radiation pressure from the star's own light pushing evenly outward

flashcards.explanation_html: Blobs of gas erupt asymmetrically from the bloated star; by Newton's third law, each ejection pushes the star in the opposite direction.

flashcards.prompt: How can pushes of only a few meters per second matter?
flashcards.back_html: They add up. Roughly 10,000 small kicks over hundreds of thousands of years can accumulate into a net speed of about 1 kilometer per second.

flashcards.prompt: What can these accumulated kicks do to a star's surroundings?
flashcards.back_html: They can unbind wide binary pairs, flinging companion stars apart — and, in rare cases, drive two stars into a collision that triggers an explosion.
